title: Java Regular Expressions
learningObjectives: Explain what a regular expression pattern describes.
Use String matches and replaceAll with regex patterns.
Use Pattern and Matcher for repeated matching.
Recognize character classes, quantifiers and anchors.
Escape regex metacharacters correctly in Java strings.

understand.concept: A regular expression (regex) describes a text pattern. Java supports regex through String methods and the Pattern and Matcher classes. Character classes such as [0-9], quantifiers such as + and *, and anchors such as ^ and $ help describe acceptable text. Regex syntax is itself embedded in Java string literals, so backslashes often need to be doubled.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic equips Java learners to write robust programs using java regular expressions in real applications.
understand.analogy: Think of each language feature as a clearly labelled tool: choose it for the specific problem it is designed to solve.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the Java language and library contracts; compile and test the actual behaviour.

explain.narrative: Use String.matches when the entire string must match the pattern. Use Pattern.compile and Matcher.find when searching within text or performing several operations. Use replaceAll for regex-based replacement, not literal replacement. Validate complex real-world formats carefully: a simple regex may check a basic shape but does not necessarily prove that an address, identifier or date is semantically valid.

examples.title: Check digits only
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("5831".matches("[0-9]+")); System.out.println("58A1".matches("[0-9]+")); } }
examples.explanation: The character class and plus quantifier require one or more digits across the whole string.

examples.title: Check a fixed prefix
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("AB123".matches("AB[0-9]{3}")); } }
examples.explanation: The {3} quantifier requires exactly three digits.

examples.title: Replace whitespace
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { String text = "Java   is fun"; System.out.println(text.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } }
examples.explanation: The regex \s+ matches one or more whitespace characters.

examples.title: Find matches
examples.explanation: Matcher.find locates successive substrings that match the pattern.

examples.title: Use anchors
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("cat".matches("^cat$")); System.out.println("a cat".matches("^cat$")); } }
examples.explanation: Anchors mark the beginning and end, requiring the entire input to be cat.

questions.answer: Whether the entire string matches the regex
options: Whether the entire string matches the regex
Whether the string contains a digit

questions.prompt: Which regex quantifier means one or more?
questions.explanation: The plus quantifier means one or more occurrences.

questions.prompt: Which class compiles a reusable regex pattern?
questions.explanation: Pattern represents a compiled regular expression.

questions.prompt: Which Matcher method searches for the next matching subsequence?
questions.explanation: find advances to the next matching subsequence.

questions.prompt: Why is \\d used in a Java regex string literal?
questions.answer: The Java string must encode the regex backslash
options: It means a literal letter d
The Java string must encode the regex backslash
It converts text to a date
questions.explanation: A Java string uses an escaped backslash to pass \d to the regex engine.
